questions.question: Explain why a ridge carved from tilted strata is always asymmetrical, defining dip, dip slope and scarp slope and giving the full reason for the difference in steepness.
questions.expected_answer: Strata are deposited horizontally and are tilted afterwards by crustal forces — folding by plate collision, unequal uplift, or the sagging of loaded basins. The dip is the angle a tilted layer makes with the horizontal. Differential erosion hollows the weak layers into valleys and leaves resistant layers as ridges, but the two faces of such a ridge are built by different rules. The dip slope is the exposed upper surface of the resistant layer itself, so it is gentle and descends at exactly the angle of dip — the same hard layer stays underfoot the whole way down. The scarp slope slices across the stack, exposing the sawn-off ends of every layer: the weak bands beneath the resistant edge wash out quickly and undermine it, so the scarp stands steep, often cliffed at the crest with debris below. The contrast is between a protected layer surface and a cut edge: the dip slope follows one layer, the scarp slope cuts across many.

questions.question: Classify cuesta, homoclinal ridge and hogsback by approximate dip angle with South African examples, and explain the geometry of cuesta basins and cuesta domes including which way the dip and scarp slopes face in each.
questions.expected_answer: The three ridges are one landform at increasing lean. Strata dipping gently, up to roughly 25 degrees, build a cuesta — strongly lopsided, with a long farmable dip slope and a short steep scarp, as in the sandstone ridge country flanking the Soutpansberg. Dips of roughly 25 to 45 degrees build a homoclinal ridge, narrower and sharper but still asymmetrical — the Magaliesberg quartzite ridge between Pretoria and Rustenburg is the celebrated example. Beyond roughly 45 degrees both faces cut across the near-vertical strata at similar steep angles, so the ridge becomes a narrow, near-symmetrical hogsback, as above the Eastern Cape village of Hogsback. The trend: steeper dip narrows the ridge and equalises its faces. In a cuesta basin the strata sag toward a centre, so the concentric resistant ridges have dip slopes facing inward and scarps facing outward; rain entering tilted aquifers at the rim gathers under pressure beneath the centre, allowing artesian boreholes. In a cuesta dome the strata arch over the centre and descend away from it, so dip slopes face outward and scarps face inward across the eroded core — the Vredefort Dome's rings are the world-famous case. In both, the dip slope faces wherever the layers lean downward.

questions.question: Describe how tilted-strata country is identified and analysed on a topographic map — contour signature, the two-gradient proof of dip direction, and vertical exaggeration — and how people use such landscapes.
questions.expected_answer: Unequal contour spacing is the signature: a cuesta or homoclinal ridge has contours packed against the scarp side of the crest and strung wide on the dip side, a hogsback has tight contours on both flanks of a thin crest, and concentric rings suggest a basin or dome. The impression is proved with a gradient on each side: with the crest at 900 metres and the 750-metre contour 300 metres away on the east but 3 000 metres away on the west, the east gradient is 150 over 300 or 1 in 2 and the west is 150 over 3 000 or 1 in 20 — so the east is the scarp and the strata dip toward the gentle western side. A cross-section perpendicular to the crest shows the ramp-against-cliff triangle profile; with a vertical scale of one centimetre to fifty metres, which is 1:5 000, against the 1:50 000 horizontal scale, the vertical exaggeration is 50 000 divided by 5 000, which is 10 times. People obey the structure: farms and plantations occupy the gentle dip slopes, towns, roads and railways follow the strike valleys, scarp faces stay wild, and crossings funnel through poorts where rivers have sawn gaps in the crest — at Olifantsnek the Hex River's breach through the Magaliesberg carries the main road and holds a dam.
